asBirthCard.p: This one comes from your birthdate and nothing else, so it says nothing about your Sun or your Rising. Add up every digit of the date you were born and yours came to sixteen exactly. There's only one road here, because the bigger totals that get added down a second time never land on sixteen. It's an uncomfortable-looking card to be handed, I know. Lightning takes the top off a tower and two people are falling out of it. But look at where it sits in the run of Majors. Just before it is The Devil, fifteen, where two people stand chained and could slip the chains off if they tried. Then sixteen, where the thing that held them gets knocked down whether they were ready or not. After it comes The Star, a woman kneeling by water at night, finally quiet. The card belongs to Mars, the planet of heat, force and cutting through, and that's its nature. It doesn't wait around to be asked.

Mostly it shows up as a low tolerance for things that are quietly wrong. At a family dinner where everyone's stepping around the obvious thing, you're the one who ends up saying it, usually over dessert, and then there's a silence you could stand a spoon in. In a meeting where a plan is being nodded through, you've already spotted the number that doesn't work, and it bothers you physically to sit on it. When a friend sends a long text explaining why everything's fine with the new boyfriend, you read it twice and can tell it isn't. You also tend to make your big changes in one go. People hear that you've quit, or moved, or cut all your hair off, and they had no idea you were even thinking about it, because for months you weren't saying anything at all.

People with this card are often the best person to have around in the first hour of a real emergency. The pipe bursts at two in the morning, a parent gets rushed to hospital, the shop's been broken into, and while everyone else is still saying they can't believe it, you're already under the sink finding the stopcock and ringing the insurer. Mars gives you that. It's a planet that's at its best when something needs doing fast. And you don't need things to go back to how they were, which frees you up a lot. A friend whose business has folded gets a very practical conversation from you about what's still standing and what could be sold, and oddly that's the one that makes them feel better. You'll happily sit with them at the kitchen table and write out an actual list.

The shadow people expect is the love of a crash. The one that actually causes trouble is the long silence before it. A lot of sixteens don't complain as they go. The flatmate leaves dishes, the manager keeps moving the deadline, your partner forgets the thing again, and you say nothing, week after week, because it doesn't seem worth the fuss. Then one ordinary Tuesday it all comes out at once, six months of it, and the other person is standing there genuinely shocked, because as far as they knew everything was fine. From their side it came out of nowhere. It didn't, of course, but they never got a chance to fix the small version. It's worth getting into the habit of saying the small thing while it's still small, even when it feels a bit petty.

When something goes badly wrong, your first move is usually to act, and act hard. You resign the same afternoon, block the number, tell your brother exactly what you think of him, put the flat on the market. It feels clean, and for a day or two there's real relief in it. A week later is often when it lands, and it tends to land in the body, bad sleep, a jaw that aches from clenching, a short fuse in the supermarket queue. That's usually also when you start wondering whether the whole thing needed burning down. The cost to the people around you is that they're living with the fallout of a decision they weren't asked about. What helps most is putting something physical between the shock and the decision. A long run, a swim, an afternoon digging out the back garden. Do that first, then make the phone call, and if you can, wait until the next morning to send anything in writing.

You tend to want the real thing early. Somewhere around the third date you ask a question most people save for month six, about the ex, the family, what they actually want from their life, and some people find that thrilling and some quietly leave. Once you're in, the less obvious thing is how loyal you are to someone who's been through a collapse with you. The partner who stayed when the job went, or drove you to the hospital at three in the morning, has you for good, and you don't forget it. The difficulty comes in the calm years. When nothing's going wrong you can start testing things, picking at a small crack to see if it holds, and a partner who likes things steady can feel they're always being checked. It helps to tell them straight when you're restless, so they know it's your mood and has very little to do with them.

You're often at your best in work where things break and someone has to fix them. Emergency departments, IT outages, the building trade, crisis comms, a turnaround job at a business that's losing money, a restaurant kitchen on a Saturday night. You're also good at the unpopular part of any project, the audit, the post-mortem, the review where somebody has to say the software isn't working and they'd be better off starting again. Where it goes wrong is slow, polite organisations where the problem everyone knows about gets discussed for eighteen months. You can find yourself either blowing it up in a meeting or quietly handing in your notice, and neither does your reputation much good. Sixteens often change careers once in a big way, usually somewhere in their thirties, and the second one tends to fit better. Keep a short written list of what's bothering you at work, and raise one item from it each month.

At twenty a sixteen has often had the ground pulled out from under them already. A family breaks up, a course or a first job goes wrong in a spectacular way, the first big relationship ends with a revelation. It can leave a young person braced, half expecting the next one. Through the twenties there's usually some self-inflicted demolition as well, walking out of things that only needed a hard conversation. By the mid-thirties most people with this card have been through two or three of these and can tell a structure that's actually rotten from one that's just annoying them. That's a big shift, and it saves a lot of wreckage. The fifties tend to bring out The Star side of it, the card that comes next. People with this number often get quieter around then, and end up as the friend others ring when their own roof falls in, because you can tell them what the morning after actually looks like.

When you feel pressure building about something and you haven't said it yet, write it on a sticky note in five words or fewer, 'Sam keeps cancelling on me', and stick it inside the kitchen cupboard door. You'll see it every time you get a mug out. Once there are two notes up about the same person or the same job, that's your cue to raise it, calmly, within the week. Take the notes down after you've had the conversation.
